https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: An image of a firefighting vehicle taking part in efforts to contain the Gironde fire, overlain with a map of the area burned. Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / EPA / Getty Images An 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde inferno By Ajit Niranjan with graphics by Lucy Swan , Harvey Symons and Paul Scruton Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he ruinous fires that overran parts of France this summer have burned more land than ever recorded, forced more people from their homes than at any point since the second world war and caused what scientists suspect is the country’s first firestorm thundercloud. The smoke from France’s biggest inferno in nearly 80 years choked Limoges, a city 125 miles (200km) from the flames, with more toxic dust than Delhi residents inhaled on the city’s worst day of smog last year. The blaze that tore through forests outside Bordeaux in late July took just a few weeks to reforge France’s relationship with fire, but the conditions behind it were centuries in the making. In the 18th century, the coastal wetlands of south-western France were so swampy that shepherds used stilts to cross them in winter. When a 1857 decree from NapoleonIII forced landowners to drain the marsh and populate it with maritime pines, the water-logged landscape was converted into Europe’s largest human-made forest. It has since become a regional economic engine running on timber that employs 30,000 people. Map of Landes de Gascogne It is also a firefighter’s nightmare. The pines that make up 90% of the trees in the Landes forest hold resin that burns like petrol, needles that carpet the ground with flammable material and cones that whiz in the wind like grenades, spreading flames across breaks in vegetation that should act as barriers. Without the diversity offered by broad-leafed species, which retain more moisture and have shady canopies that stop vegetation from drying, the dense monoculture can burn with fury when sparks catch. View image in fullscreen Pine trees burn near Marcheprime outside Bordeaux on 26 July. Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP That is what happened in 1949, when a blaze that began in a saw mill burned 50,000 hectares. Gorging on plentiful fuel and with few breaks to impede their spread, the flames killed 82 people, most of them volunteers racing to put out the fire. It remains Europe’s deadliest wildfire. Firefighting capacity has vastly improved since, but the potential for disaster has continued to increase. Humanity has fouled the atmosphere with 1.85tn tonnes of planet-baking carbon since the 1857 decree, warming Europe by 2.4C and increasing the risk of hot and dry extremes that were once unthinkable. A strikingly wet winter in western Europe this year helped plants grow tall, only for relentless heatwaves to later strip them of moisture, creating a large fuel surplus for fires to devour. By mid-July, temperatures across France had reached record highs and soil moisture had fallen to record lows, setting the stage for the Gironde inferno. Chart showing record breaking heat and drought conditions in France Not long after noon on 22 July, after three straight weeks of more than 30C heat, smoke rose from the tightly packed pine stands near Saumos, a village 20 miles west of Bordeaux. The source of ignition is under investigation, but workers contracted by Enedis, a utility company that manages France’s electricity distribution, were active in the area and reported having sparked a fire with a faulty machine. The Bordeaux public prosecutor, which has identified the machine as its leading line of inquiry, did not respond to requests for comment. Enedis declined to answer specific questions because of the continuing investigation. ‘We stared into an abyss’: the men and women battling France’s megafire Read more Most wildfires are started by humans through actions such as dropping cigarette butts, failing to properly extinguish campfires or dispose of barbecues. Public awareness campaigns to discourage reckless behaviour are thought to have contributed to a fall in the number of fires in southern Europe since the 1980s but preventing arson is much harder. French police have arrested nearly 500 people on suspicion of starting fires since the start of the summer, about 70% of which are thought to have been deliberate. Once a fire has begun, it is weather and geography that dictate whether it will quickly wither or morph into a hellish blaze. Outside Saumos, it was immediately clear that firefighters were facing the latter. The fire engulfed several hundreds of hectares in a matter of hours and reached the outskirts of La Porge, which would lose one in 10 homes to the flames in the days that followed. Within 24 hours of the initial spark, southerly winds had pushed the fire’s southern front to Cap Ferret, an upmarket peninsula known as the Hamptons of France, nine miles away. map Helping the fire’s rapid spread was its location in an area that had been flattened by a powerful storm in 1999 and then swiftly replanted, resulting in a uniform tree height that created a continuous fuel load. But the response in those crucial early hours has also been criticised. Local forestry workers told Le Monde that firefighters had rejected their recommendation to quickly set a controlled burn, while residents of La Porge claim resources were taken from their village to protect the wealthier Cap Ferret. The Gironde fire service, which did not respond to requests for comment, has said it had done all it could to stop the fire and rejected allegations that it abandoned La Porge. Bruno Lafon, the head of the regional forest fire prevention service, an association of forestry workers who work with firefighters to prevent blazes, said he could understand that volunteers who saw their livelihoods go up in flames wanted more help to have come. But, he said, the powerful combination of drought, heat and wind made the initial spread extremely hard to stop. “The men on the ground did what they could, though I think it would have taken a greater number of planes from the beginning,” he said. The French government has also been criticised because maintenance work meant only seven of its 12 water-bombing planes were available at the peak of the fire. View image in fullscreen Wildfires evacuees at an exhibition centre in Bordeaux. Photograph: Alain Jocard/AFP/Getty Images As the fire torched more land, authorities acted quickly to get people to safety. The first evacuations began on the afternoon of 22 July, when 100 residents of the north-eastern quarter of La Porge were taken to shelter in a community hall. Overnight, that number rose to more than 10,000, and just a few days later it had reached nearly 220,000. Across France and neighbouring Spain, which was also battling extreme wildfires, evacuation orders covered more than 300,000 people, a peacetime displacement unprecedented in Europe. Some residents returned to charred possessions, burnt-out homes and shells of cars, but the evacuations proved hugely successful. Not a single person died as a direct result of the Gironde fire, though four firefighters lost their lives tackling separate blazes across the country last month. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A resident of Le Porge inspects damage caused by the fire. Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images Among the evacuees was Hervé Jactel, a forest scientist at INRAE, a public research institute, who was forced to flee twice in two days. Watching Nasa maps with apprehension as the fire drew near, he lost a 20-year experiment investigating the diversity of forest trees as a result of burning biomass that jumped a cornfield. He said the fire had not come as a surprise. “From an ecological and forest management point of view, everything was in place to increase the risk of a very large fire,” he said. “Not only because of the climate, but because of the amount and homogeneity of the fuel.” Scientists suspect those conditions resulted in the extreme levels of energy that generated a firecloud, a powerful chimney of smoke stretching into the atmosphere that creates its own weather system. Known as a pyrocumulonimbus cloud , , it can spit lightning, and rain down burning embers that spark new blazes and spread the fire further. Nasa has described them as fire-breathing dragons. The true danger, however, lay not in the apocalyptic fire cloud but in the pollutants that it dispersed. map Studies have found wildfire smoke to be responsible for 1.5 million deaths around the world each year, making it one of the deadliest environmental threats to human health. Initially, much of the smoke blew straight out over the Atlantic Ocean, but a shift in wind direction caused it to choke Bordeaux, which was nervously watching the approaching inferno, before drifting over Angoulême and Limoges. It clogged the air with so much soot and ash that daily concentrations of airway-inflaming particles hit highs rarely seen, even in cities as polluted as Delhi. graph A shift in the weather helped firefighters halt the advance of the blaze at 42,000 hectares of burned area at the end of July. In the days since, they have continued to put out small flare-ups and smouldering “zombie fires” underground that they say could continue to return for months. Scientists fear for the forest’s short-term recovery. Fire can trigger outbreaks of bark beetles, which attack damaged trees and increase the fuel load for the next fire – a vicious cycle already well documented in California. The burned wood also attracts the invasive pine nematode, a microscopic worm that had arrived in south-west France in November. It blocks the flow of sap in trees, causing them to wilt and die within months. The greatest threats to the forest, however, are yet to come. Fire weather is projected to become increasingly severe across Europe as carbon pollution continues to heat the planet. Without action to improve fire management, the burned area in Europe is predicted to rise by 39% even in a best-scenario scenario for cutting pollution. In a worst-case scenario, it could nearly triple. Experts have called for rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and better management of the land, such as breaking up continuous tracts of forest and diversifying tree species. https://wpde.com/news/nation-world/trump.text: The Trump administration will consider pulling U.S. troops from Europe, according to a report. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will receive at least four distinct options for American troop dispositions in Europe by Nov. 6, ahead of the December completion deadline for the review, per internal Pentagon documents, the Independent reported . The six-month evaluation that launched in June has concerned NATO allies. The European countries fear that the roughly 80,000 U.S. troops deployed across the continent will be substantially reduced, along with potential retaliation against nations that President Trump believes failed to adequately support the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. A key part of framing the formal options submitted to Hegseth involves a decision briefing scheduled for Sept. 18 between the top U.S. general in Europe and the Pentagon's policy chief, Elbridge Colby, according to the document. Colby is expected to brief NATO ambassadors on the progress of the review on Thursday at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels. An anonymous senior Defense Department official told Reuters regarding the review, "We want to be able to talk through the pros and cons of a variety of different force levels or dispositions." The Trump administration has repeatedly indicated that it intends to scale back U.S. military commitments in Europe, urging NATO allies to take on more of the responsibility. Trump has also expressed frustration over allies relying on U.S. security guarantees while allegedly not providing sufficient backing for the Iran conflict, including nations delaying or denying overflight and basing permissions for American warplanes. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte acknowledged Trump's disappointment, but noted that the vast majority of European allies provided meaningful assistance. The Pentagon official explained that the Trump administration has clearly communicated its strategy, saying, "we are transitioning to provide critical, more limited support with allies in the lead." "President Trump has also been quite rightly and clearly frustrated with certain allies' behavior in recent months. So there's clearly at least some demand signal to have options that would show us (downgrading) our force levels in Europe," the official added. The review aims to "provide a spectrum of options from where we are to wherever" the assessment leads, according to the official. When announcing the review in June, Hegseth rebuked certain "free-riding" NATO members, emphasizing that the process would ensure U.S. "access, basing, and overflight are clearly delineated." According to the document, the DOD's internal Terms of Reference extend beyond basic access, basing, and overflight (ABO) agreements to include space, cyber, and "intelligence architectures and infrastructure that enable U.S. global power projection." The senior official said that expanding the definition of ABO ensures the Trump administration accounts for the full range of support provided by host nations. The guidelines also evaluate whether allies are progressing toward meeting NATO defense spending pledges and addressing shortfalls in the NATO Force Model following earlier U.S. drawdown announcements . The Trump administration sent allies a questionnaire regarding defense strategies, procurement, and alignment with U.S. foreign policy. "What if any restrictions has the country placed on U.S. access, basing, and overflight (ABO)? If so, why? Are they willing to reduce or eliminate any such restrictions?" the questionnaire asks. "Has the country publicly opposed regulations or other measures designed to inhibit or reduce transatlantic defense industrial cooperation? If so, how? If not, would they be willing to do so?" another question reads. Allies are to respond by Friday. "We are working very, very hard, and it is a relatively tight timeline," the DOD official said. "A lot of prior analysis will inform this, which should allow us to move quicker on our end." This comes as CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow this week, warning Russian officials not to escalate conflict with the U.S.'s NATO allies, in particular Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, in response to Russia’s stalemated invasion of Ukraine, two unnamed sources told Politico . Ratcliffe also used the trip to press Russia to reduce military and economic support for Iran, according to one of the two sources and a U.K. official. On Wednesday, Trump denied speculation that Ratcliffe made the trip to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin not to test NATO’s resolve or attack the U.K., which this week vowed to double down on its support for Ukraine. Trump said the visit was “semi-routine,” but acknowledged it was about ending the war. “I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84g.text: Image source, DSNS Ukraine Image caption, Four people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a business centre in Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 25 September 2026, 19:02 BST Updated 14 minutes ago President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people. "All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said. On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said he was an Israeli citizen. Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence. About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes. Some firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad. In the north-western city of Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv". In Friday's social media post, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers â for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target. "It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror." Late on Friday, Zelensky said "additional decisions" had been made at his meeting with Ukraine's top defence and security officials to protect the country's data centres and other critical communications facilities to ensure their continuous operation. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres. "Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said. Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs. But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access". Image source, DSNS Kyiv Image caption, A 14-year-old boy, an Israeli citizen, was killed when a Russian drone hit a multi-storey residential building in Kyiv's central Pecherskyi district The data centre hit by Russia on Friday was run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after the daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites". Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said on Friday evening that seven people had been killed and 59 injured after Russian overnight attacks. Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence. Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC. The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi. In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure â seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches. Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water Published 1 day ago Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial Published 4 days ago Speaking to reporters late on Friday, Putin said Moscow would "give careful thought" to the idea of resuming direct peace negotiations with Kyiv, citing last week's "massive" Ukrainian attack on the capital Moscow and other recent strikes. "It's all possible," he said, but stressed that Ukraine "must feel our retaliatory strikes", and that all decisions would be taken "based on the Russian Federation's interests". Zelensky had earlier said he was ready for trilateral talks that would also involve the US. Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly accused Putin of rejecting any peace negotiations, saying he was seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory. Speaking to the media, Putin also restated his position that Moscow had "no plans" and "no reason" to attack Europe. He had made similar statements about Ukraine, before launching his full-scale invasion almost five years ago. In a separate development on Friday, the European Union agreed to release â¬6.6bn for Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, describing this as "good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia". This includes â¬900 million for the EU's Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine, and a â¬1 billion fund for joint procurement of equipment, she said on X. "Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite." Meanwhile, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday. In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented. The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals. In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies. Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport , while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites . https://24.hu/belfold/2026/11/09/nyiregy.text: Egy 20 éves fiatal meghalt, barátja megsérült, amikor hétfő hajnalban egy autó a parkoló kocsijukba csapódott egy nyíregyházi benzinkúton. Az RTL Híradó úgy tudja, az érkező autós a megengedett sebesség sokszorosával száguldott, majd kisodródott és a benzinkút parkolójába repült, miután megdobta egy padka. A csatorna beszámolója szerint a becsapódás helyétől több tíz méteren át tolta maga előtt a balesetet okozó autó a másik járművet. A tragédiát előidéző autószerelő részeg lehetett. A rendőrség tájékoztatása szerint a 34 éves nyíregyházi férfinél ugyanis felmerült az ittasság gyanúja. Letartóztatását kezdeményezik, ezt a kórházban közölték vele.
